\subsection{Counting collapses at a finite $k^\ast$}

Figure~\ref{fig:main}(a) shows counting accuracy against $k$. Every model
reproduces the shape the theorem predicts: accuracy is high for small $k$, then
falls to a floor and stays there. Pooled over the panel, accuracy is
\AccRepLow{}\% at $k\le3$ and \AccRepHigh{}\% at $k\ge6$. Past the collapse point
the errors are not random: at $k\ge8$, \LoopPct{}\% of generations run long
(looping or overcounting) and \TruncPct{}\% stop short --- precisely the two
behaviours available to a decoder whose stop decision has lost access to the
count.

The collapse point $k^\ast$ ranges from \kStarMin{} to \kStarMax{}
(Table~\ref{tab:models}); within the Qwen3-TTS family it doubles from $0.6$B to
$1.7$B, so scale buys a longer horizon but a bounded one, as
\eqref{eq:horizon} says it should. The unit of repetition can be a word, a whole
sentence, or a place-value pattern (\emph{six hundred sixty-six thousand six
hundred sixty-six}); all three produce the same curve. What matters is that it
recurs.

\subsection{The limit is periodicity, not length}

Figure~\ref{fig:main}(b) is the paper's sharpest test. Each control item has the
same carrier sentence and the same word count as its repeated twin, and differs
only in that the $k$ copies of one word are replaced by $k$ distinct words. If
the failure were about sequence length, attention span, or accumulated exposure
bias, the two curves would coincide. They do not: at $k\ge6$, repeated items are
rendered correctly \AccRepHigh{}\% $[\AccRepHighLo{}, \AccRepHighHi{}]$ of the
time against \AccCtlHigh{}\% $[\AccCtlHighLo{}, \AccCtlHighHi{}]$ for controls
(Wilson intervals, $n=\AccRepHighN{}$ generations per condition, panel only).
Models that cannot say \emph{very} six times in a row will say twelve or sixteen
\emph{different} adverbs without difficulty.

One alternative deserves ruling out: repeated text is unusual text, so perhaps
models fail on it because it is improbable rather than because it is periodic.
That would require the controls to be the more natural member of each pair. They
are not. Scored under a general-purpose causal LM, the control is the \emph{less}
probable member in \NllCtlHigherPct{}\% of the \NllPairs{} matched pairs (mean
per-token NLL \NllCtl{} vs.\ \NllRep{}), and the gap widens monotonically with
$k$. The harder-to-predict text is the one models render correctly, so
naturalness runs opposite to the effect.

A second alternative locates the collapse in acoustic rather than text space: an
attractor reached once enough near-identical frames accumulate, with the text
playing no part. That predicts a horizon counted in tokens, so sentence
repetition --- whose unit costs several times more tokens than a word --- should
collapse after far fewer repetitions. It does not. Across \UnitNModels{} models
$k^\ast$ differs between the two families by \UnitKDiff{} repetitions on average
while the token count at collapse differs by \UnitTokRatio{}$\times$. The horizon
is counted in applications of the periodic map, the unit
Theorem~\ref{thm:collapse} says it should be.

\subsection{The states the decoder visits stop multiplying}

Theorem~\ref{thm:collapse}(ii) says the states a decoder visits under periodic
conditioning stop being mutually distinguishable, so asking for more repetitions
should stop buying it distinct internal states while the same amount of
non-repetitive text keeps buying them. We count distinguishable states by the
effective rank $\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{eff}} = \exp(-\sum_i p_i \log p_i)$ of the
generation trajectory over normalised singular values; the statistic is the
\emph{capacity gain} $\mathrm{d}\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{eff}}/\mathrm{d}\log k$,
with intervals bootstrapped over stimulus templates.

Figure~\ref{fig:main}(c,d) shows the result. On repeated text the capacity gain
is a factor \CapRatio{} of the control gain, with disjoint 95\% intervals for
\NCapSepWord{} of the \NCapModels{} panel checkpoints; the matched-pair form of
the comparison gives a positive gap in \CapFracPos{}\% of pairs.

An obvious objection is that this is circular: if a model correctly renders
\emph{very} sixteen times the audio really is monotonous, so a low-rank
trajectory would follow from the stimulus rather than from any loss of capacity.
Two checks say otherwise. Adding realised output diversity --- type/token ratio
over emitted acoustic tokens, the rate at which a token repeats its predecessor,
and length --- as covariates leaves the ratio at \CapAdjRatio{}. Restricting to
the items each model rendered \emph{correctly}, where the audio is by
construction what was asked for, leaves it at \CapCorrRatio{}
($\CapCorrN{}$ checkpoints with sufficient correct items). The decoder does not
merely make mistakes on repeated text --- it runs out of internal states in which
a mistake and a correct continuation could differ.

Lemma~\ref{lem:dilution} concerns the softmax \emph{restricted to the $k$ repeated
keys}: raw attention weight is normalised over the whole sequence, whose length
grows with $k$, confounding dilution with sequence growth. Renormalised over the
occurrence columns, the profile entropy grows with $\log k$ at slope
\BlockEntropySlope{}, the implied spread is $\delta \le 0.06$ nats across the
ladder, and no occurrence --- not even the most attended --- captures more than
$1.9/k$ of the block's mass. Attention over the repeated spans is within a few
percent of uniform, which is what Assumption~\ref{ass:periodic} needs.

\subsection{Two things we could not establish}
\label{sec:negative}

We first tried to estimate $q$ directly, locating repetition boundaries from text
attention and fitting $\log\lVert h_{m+1}-h_m\rVert = a + m\log q$. That
estimator is unsound here: localisation needs a monotone text read-head, and
these decoders' deep-layer attention centroid advances on barely half of
generation steps, so boundary estimates collapse onto near-duplicate positions
and the distances measure localisation error. The failure is self-defeating by
construction --- the flatter the attention over repeated spans, exactly what
Lemma~\ref{lem:dilution} predicts, the worse any attention-based localiser gets.
The capacity measure needs no boundaries, which is why we adopted it.

Second, we cannot claim the count is \emph{absent}. A ridge probe recovering
$\log_2 k$ from trajectory summaries decodes it only coarsely (median
$R^2 = \ProbeLateRTwo{}$ late in generation), and contrasting the first and last
third of the \emph{same} trajectory --- so that probe capacity cancels --- the
count is retained at \ProbeRetRep{} of its early level on repeated text against
\ProbeRetCtl{} on controls, repeated being lower in \ProbeNBelowWord{} of
\ProbeNModels{} variants. Consistent in direction, but this is degradation, not
erasure.
